claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is responsible for more than 1 million deaths each year.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of human tuberculosis (TB), is responsible for more than 1 million deaths each year and the bacterium currently infects nearly ~1.5 billion individuals.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the introduction without specific citation, drawing from established knowledge about TB burden.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis currently infects nearly 1.5 billion individuals.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of human tuberculosis (TB), is responsible for more than 1 million deaths each year and the bacterium currently infects nearly ~1.5 billion individuals.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the introduction without specific citation, drawing from established knowledge about TB infection prevalence.

claim: Most TB infections (~90%) remain in a latent or asymptomatic state.
source: A hallmark of TB is that infected individuals rarely develop active TB disease and most infections (~90%) remain in a latent or asymptomatic state.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge about TB disease progression.

claim: Mtb's ability to metabolize host-derived lipids (fatty acids and cholesterol) is thought to enable bacterial persistence for long periods of time.
source: Mtb is exquisitely adapted to survive within the human host and the bacterium's ability to metabolize host-derived lipids (fatty acids and cholesterol) is thought to enable bacterial persistence for long periods of time.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the role of lipid metabolism in persistence, indicated by 'is thought to'.

claim: In the 1950s, it was determined that Mtb propagated in mammalian tissues preferentially metabolizes fatty acids.
source: In the 1950s, it was determined that Mtb propagated in mammalian tissues preferentially metabolizes fatty acids (Bloch and Segal, 1956) and numerous studies since have repeatedly demonstrated that lipid metabolism promotes Mtb survival during infection (Marrero et al., 2010; McKinney et al., 2000; Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bloch and Segal, 1956.

claim: Lipid metabolism promotes Mtb survival during infection.
source: In the 1950s, it was determined that Mtb propagated in mammalian tissues preferentially metabolizes fatty acids (Bloch and Segal, 1956) and numerous studies since have repeatedly demonstrated that lipid metabolism promotes Mtb survival during infection (Marrero et al., 2010; McKinney et al., 2000; Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Marrero et al., 2010; McKinney et al., 2000; Muñoz-Elías et al., 2006).

claim: Mtb has the ability to metabolize cholesterol.
source: Mtb also has the ability to metabolize cholesterol (Van der Geize et al., 2007) and the utilization of this nutrient is critical for Mtb survival within macrophages (VanderVen et al., 2015) and in various in vivo infection models (Chang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2010; Nesbitt et al., 2010; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Yam et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Van der Geize et al., 2007.

claim: Cholesterol utilization is critical for Mtb survival within macrophages.
source: Mtb also has the ability to metabolize cholesterol (Van der Geize et al., 2007) and the utilization of this nutrient is critical for Mtb survival within macrophages (VanderVen et al., 2015) and in various in vivo infection models (Chang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2010; Nesbitt et al., 2010; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Yam et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to VanderVen et al., 2015.

claim: Cholesterol utilization is critical for Mtb survival in various in vivo infection models.
source: Mtb also has the ability to metabolize cholesterol (Van der Geize et al., 2007) and the utilization of this nutrient is critical for Mtb survival within macrophages (VanderVen et al., 2015) and in various in vivo infection models (Chang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2010; Nesbitt et al., 2010; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Yam et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Chang et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2010; Nesbitt et al., 2010; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Yam et al., 2009).

claim: The Mtb genome does not encode canonical fatty acid transporters that are typically found in other bacterial systems.
source: The mycolic acid-containing cell envelope of Mtb constitutes a unique barrier for the import of hydrophobic molecules and likely explains why the Mtb genome does not encode canonical fatty acid transporters that are typically found in other bacterial systems (Black et al., 1987; Theodoulou et al., 2016; van den Berg et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Black et al., 1987; Theodoulou et al., 2016; van den Berg et al., 2004).

claim: Mtb uses Mce proteins to import hydrophobic nutrients across the bacterial cell envelope.
source: Instead, it is thought that Mtb uses Mce proteins to import hydrophobic nutrients across the bacterial cell envelope.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'it is thought that'.

claim: The Mce family of proteins in Mtb were originally associated with mammalian cell entry.
source: The Mce family of proteins in Mtb were originally associated with mammalian cell entry (Arruda et al., 1993) and are classified as part of the MlaD superfamily (cl27420) based on the presence of one or more Mce domains (Casali and Riley, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arruda et al., 1993.

claim: Mce proteins are classified as part of the MlaD superfamily (cl27420) based on the presence of one or more Mce domains.
source: The Mce family of proteins in Mtb were originally associated with mammalian cell entry (Arruda et al., 1993) and are classified as part of the MlaD superfamily (cl27420) based on the presence of one or more Mce domains (Casali and Riley, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Casali and Riley, 2007.

claim: Proteins containing Mce domains have been implicated in the transport of hydrophobic molecules in various bacteria and chloroplasts.
source: Proteins containing Mce domains have been implicated in the transport of hydrophobic molecules in various bacteria and chloroplasts (Awai et al., 2006; Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Mohn et al., 2008; Roston et al., 2011; Sutterlin et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Awai et al., 2006; Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Mohn et al., 2008; Roston et al., 2011; Sutterlin et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2008).

claim: Mce proteins mediate transport of hydrophobic molecules across double-membranous structures in cells.
source: The aggregate data now indicate that Mce proteins mediate transport of hydrophobic molecules across double-membranous structures in cells (Ekiert et al., 2017; Thong et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Ekiert et al., 2017; Thong et al., 2016).

claim: Mtb imports cholesterol across the mycobacterial cell envelope via the multi-subunit Mce transporter, termed Mce4.
source: Mtb imports cholesterol across the mycobacterial cell envelope via the multi-subunit Mce transporter, termed Mce4 (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008) and the Mtb genome contains four total unlinked mce loci (mce1-mce4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pandey and Sassetti, 2008.

claim: The Mtb genome contains four total unlinked mce loci (mce1-mce4).
source: Mtb imports cholesterol across the mycobacterial cell envelope via the multi-subunit Mce transporter, termed Mce4 (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008) and the Mtb genome contains four total unlinked mce loci (mce1-mce4).
evidence: This is a statement of genomic fact about Mtb.

claim: Most of the genes required for the growth of Mtb on cholesterol as a sole carbon source have been mapped.
source: Most of the genes required for the growth of Mtb on cholesterol as a sole carbon source have been mapped (Griffin et al., 2011) but, little is known about how Mtb utilizes cholesterol in the presence of other nutrients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2011.

claim: Mtb can co-metabolize simple carbon substrates in vitro.
source: Mtb can co-metabolize simple carbon substrates in vitro (de Carvalho et al., 2010), which suggests that the bacterium has the capacity to utilize fatty acids and cholesterol simultaneously in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: Mtb has the capacity to utilize fatty acids and cholesterol simultaneously in vivo.
source: Mtb can co-metabolize simple carbon substrates in vitro (de Carvalho et al., 2010), which suggests that the bacterium has the capacity to utilize fatty acids and cholesterol simultaneously in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on in vitro co-metabolism data, indicated by 'suggests'.

claim: Mtb can induce foamy macrophage formation and can reside within these fatty acid and cholesterol-loaded cells.
source: For example, Mtb can induce foamy macrophage formation and can reside within these fatty acid and cholesterol-loaded cells (Peyron et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peyron et al., 2008.

claim: Mtb is capable of persisting within the necrotic centers of human granulomas, an environment that is rich in fatty acids and cholesterol.
source: It is also thought that Mtb is capable of persisting within the necrotic centers of human granulomas, an environment that is rich in fatty acids and cholesterol (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'it is thought that', supported by citation to Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Mtb utilizes fatty acids to balance the incorporation of cholesterol-derived metabolic intermediates into biosynthesis of bacterial cell wall lipids when growing in macrophages.
source: Mtb also has the capacity to metabolically integrate the utilization of fatty acids and cholesterol when growing in macrophages where Mtb utilizes fatty acids to balance the incorporation of cholesterol-derived metabolic intermediates into biosynthesis of bacterial cell wall lipids (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Rv3723/LucA is required for the import of both fatty acids and cholesterol by Mtb during growth in macrophages and in axenic culture.
source: We identified Rv3723, a protein of unknown function and determined that this protein is required for the import of both fatty acids and cholesterol by Mtb during growth in macrophages and in axenic culture.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LucA facilitates fatty acid and cholesterol uptake in Mtb by stabilizing protein subunits of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters.
source: We determined that LucA facilitates fatty acid and cholesterol uptake in Mtb by stabilizing protein subunits of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Mce1 complex transports fatty acids into Mtb.
source: These studies also establish that the Mce1 complex transports fatty acids into Mtb and that LucA is required for full virulence in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LucA is required for full virulence in vivo.
source: These studies also establish that the Mce1 complex transports fatty acids into Mtb and that LucA is required for full virulence in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fatty acid and cholesterol assimilation are inexorably linked in Mtb.
source: These data establish that fatty acid and cholesterol assimilation are inexorably linked in Mtb and reveals a key function for Rv3723/LucA in in coordinating thetransport of both these substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The Mtb H37Rv mutant (Δicl1::hyg) has a synthetic lethal phenotype and fails to grow in rich media containing cholesterol.
source: To do this, we used the Mtb H37Rv mutant (Δicl1::hyg) (McKinney et al., 2000) which has a synthetic lethal phenotype and fails to grow in rich media containing cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKinney et al., 2000.

claim: The growth inhibition of Δicl1::hyg is linked to the accumulation of one or more toxic cholesterol-derived intermediates produced by the methylcitrate cycle.
source: This growth inhibition is linked to the accumulation of one or more toxic cholesterol-derived intermediates produced by the methylcitrate cycle, which accumulate in the bacteria when icl1 is nonfunctional (Eoh and Rhee, 2014; Lee et al., 2013; VanderVen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Eoh and Rhee, 2014; Lee et al., 2013; VanderVen et al., 2015).

claim: 133 transposon rescue mutants were isolated in a Δicl1::hyg background that gained the ability to grow on media containing cholesterol.
source: Therefore, we isolated transposon rescue mutants in a Δicl1::hyg background that gained the ability to grow on media containing cholesterol. In total, 133 clones were isolated and the mutations were mapped to 19 separate genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the forward genetic screen.

claim: The mutations in the transposon rescue mutants were mapped to 19 separate genes.
source: Therefore, we isolated transposon rescue mutants in a Δicl1::hyg background that gained the ability to grow on media containing cholesterol. In total, 133 clones were isolated and the mutations were mapped to 19 separate genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the forward genetic screen, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The rescue phenotype was confirmed for 16 of the 19 mutants in liquid media containing cholesterol.
source: The rescue phenotype was further confirmed for 16 of the 19 mutants in liquid media containing cholesterol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result confirming the rescue phenotype, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nine of the 16 identified genes had been predicted to be required for growth of Mtb on cholesterol as a sole carbon source.
source: Nine of the 16 identified genes had been predicted to be required for growth of Mtb on cholesterol as a sole carbon source (Griffin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2011.

claim: Inactivating rv1130/prpD and rv1131/prpC most likely limits production of the toxic methylcitrate cycle intermediate(s) that accumulate in the absence of icl1.
source: Inactivating rv1130/prpD and rv1131/prpC most likely limits production of the toxic methylcitrate cycle intermediate(s) that accumulate in the absence of icl1 and this allows growth of these mutants (Eoh and Rhee, 2014; VanderVen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of rescue, supported by citations (Eoh and Rhee, 2014; VanderVen et al., 2015).

claim: Mutations in genes encoding cholesterol catabolic enzymes rv3545c/cyp125, rv3568c/hsaC, and rv3570c/hsaA likely rescue growth by reducing the amount of propionyl-CoA released from cholesterol that can feed into the methylcitrate cycle.
source: This screen also identified mutations in genes encoding cholesterol catabolic enzymes rv3545c/cyp125, rv3568c/hsaC, and rv3570c/hsaA (Capyk et al., 2009; Dresen et al., 2010; Yam et al., 2009). These mutations likely rescue growth by reducing the amount of propionyl-CoA released from cholesterol that can feed into the methylcitrate cycle.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of rescue, supported by citations (Capyk et al., 2009; Dresen et al., 2010; Yam et al., 2009).

claim: Chemically inhibiting the PrpC or the HsaAB enzymes is sufficient to rescue growth of the Δicl1::hyg mutant in cholesterol media.
source: These findings are consistent with the observation that chemically inhibiting the PrpC or the HsaAB enzymes is sufficient to rescue growth of the Δicl1::hyg mutant in cholesterol media (VanderVen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to VanderVen et al., 2015.

claim: Seventeen sibling mutants carrying Himar transposon insertions in the lucA gene were identified with the screen.
source: Seventeen sibling mutants carrying Himar transposon insertions in the lucA gene (Δicl1::hyg, lucA::TnHimar) were identified with the screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that lucA is required for cholesterol utilization by Mtb.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the screen, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: lucA is required for cholesterol utilization by Mtb.
source: Seventeen sibling mutants carrying Himar transposon insertions in the lucA gene (Δicl1::hyg, lucA::TnHimar) were identified with the screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that lucA is required for cholesterol utilization by Mtb.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results, indicated by 'suggesting'.

claim: Orthologs of lucA are restricted to Mycobacterium spp.
source: Orthologs of lucA are restricted to Mycobacterium spp., and this gene encodes an uncharacterized putative integral membrane protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic distribution of lucA orthologs.

claim: lucA encodes an uncharacterized putative integral membrane protein.
source: Orthologs of lucA are restricted to Mycobacterium spp., and this gene encodes an uncharacterized putative integral membrane protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the predicted function of the lucA gene product.

claim: Previous genetic epistasis studies implicated lucA in cholesterol utilization in vivo.
source: Additionally, previous genetic epistasis studies implicated lucA in cholesterol utilization in vivo (Joshi et al., 2006), but, the function of this gene/protein has not yet been described.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2006.

claim: Complementation with lucA restores cholesterol toxicity in the Δicl1::hyg lucA::TnHimar mutant.
source: Using genetic complementation, we confirmed that the transposon insertion in the lucA gene is responsible for the growth rescue of the Δicl1::hyg, lucA::TnHimar mutant in cholesterol-containing media (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from genetic complementation, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: LucA-GFP has a peripheral distribution consistent with a cell membrane or cell envelope localization.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed a peripheral distribution for LucA-GFP, which is consistent with LucA having a cell membrane or cell envelope localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from confocal microscopy, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant has a 90% reduction in the amount of 14CO2 released from [4-14C]-cholesterol relative to the wild-type and the complemented strains.
source: This assay detected a 90% reduction in the amount of 14CO2 released from [4-14C]-cholesterol in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant relative to the wild-type and the complemented strains (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from radiorespirometry assay, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant assimilates 70% less cholesterol relative to the wild-type and complemented controls.
source: We found that the ΔlucA::hyg mutant assimilates 70% less cholesterol relative to the wild-type and complemented controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from cholesterol uptake assay, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The levels of cholesterol metabolism and uptake in the ΔlucA::hyg strain was comparable to a Mtb Erdman mutant lacking the permease subunit of the Mce4 cholesterol transporter Rv3501c/YrbE4A (ΔyrbE4A::hyg).
source: The levels of cholesterol metabolism and uptake in the ΔlucA::hyg strain was comparable to a Mtb Erdman mutant lacking the permease subunit of the Mce4 cholesterol transporter Rv3501c/YrbE4A (ΔyrbE4A::hyg) (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of experimental results, with reference to Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The residual cholesterol that is imported in the ΔyrbE4A::hyg mutant may be transported by an unknown alternative cholesterol transporter in Mtb.
source: The residual cholesterol that is imported in the ΔyrbE4A::hyg mutant may be transported by an unknown alternative cholesterol transporter in Mtb.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'may be'.

claim: The KstR regulon was strongly down-regulated in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant during macrophage infection.
source: These experiments revealed that the KstR regulon was strongly down-regulated in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from transcriptional profiling, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The KstR regulon is controlled by the transcriptional repressor, KstR which regulates expression of the genes encoding enzymes responsible for metabolizing the side chain and A/B rings of cholesterol.
source: The KstR regulon is controlled by the transcriptional repressor, KstR which regulates expression of the genes encoding enzymes responsible for metabolizing the side chain and A/B rings of cholesterol (Kendall et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kendall et al., 2007.

claim: The KstR regulon is activated in a 'feed forward' manner when KstR is de-repressed by binding to the second cholesterol degradation intermediate, 3-oxocholest-4-en-26-oyl-CoA (3OCh-CoA).
source: The KstR regulon is activated in a 'feed forward' manner when KstR is de-repressed by binding to the second cholesterol degradation intermediate, 3-oxocholest-4-en-26-oyl-CoA (3OCh-CoA) (Ho et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2016.

claim: Down-regulation of the KstR regulon in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is consistent with a decrease in cholesterol uptake by the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: Thus, down-regulation of the KstR regulon in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is consistent with a decrease in cholesterol uptake by the ΔlucA::hyg mutant and suggests that 3OCh-CoA may not be produced to levels that are sufficient to de-repress the KstR regulon in the mutant during infection in macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the transcriptional data to cholesterol uptake.

claim: 3OCh-CoA may not be produced to levels that are sufficient to de-repress the KstR regulon in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant during infection in macrophages.
source: Thus, down-regulation of the KstR regulon in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is consistent with a decrease in cholesterol uptake by the ΔlucA::hyg mutant and suggests that 3OCh-CoA may not be produced to levels that are sufficient to de-repress the KstR regulon in the mutant during infection in macrophages.
evidence: This is a speculative inference indicated by 'suggests' and 'may not'.

claim: Expression of the methyl-malonyl and the methylcitrate cycle genes were down-regulated in the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: We found that expression of the methyl-malonyl and the methylcitrate cycle genes were also down-regulated in the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from transcriptional profiling, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Mtb propionyl-CoA, activates the rv1130/prpD promoter to enhance the bacterium's ability to assimilate cholesterol-derived metabolic intermediates via the methyl-citrate pathway.
source: In Mtb propionyl-CoA, activates the rv1130/prpD promoter to enhance the bacterium's ability to assimilate cholesterol-derived metabolic intermediates via the methyl-citrate pathway (Griffin et al., 2012; Masiewicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Griffin et al., 2012; Masiewicz et al., 2012).

claim: GFP fluorescence increased >20 fold in wild-type Mtb when the bacteria were grown in media containing cholesterol or propionate.
source: We validated this reporter strain and determined by flow cytometry that GFP fluorescence increased >20 fold in wild-type Mtb when the bacteria were grown in media containing cholesterol or propionate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from flow cytometry, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: There was a ~75% reduction in GFP fluorescence in the ΔlucA::hyg strain relative to the wild type and complemented strain controls when the bacteria were grown in media containing cholesterol.
source: Using this reporter, we observed a ~75% reduction in GFP fluorescence in the ΔlucA::hyg strain relative to the wild type and complemented strain controls when the bacteria were grown in media containing cholesterol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from flow cytometry, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a ~ 75% reduction in GFP fluorescence in the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg strain during infection in macrophages.
source: This analysis also demonstrated a ~ 75% reduction in GFP fluorescence in the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) supporting the idea that the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant is defective in assimilating cholesterol during infection in macrophages.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from flow cytometry, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant is defective in assimilating cholesterol during infection in macrophages.
source: This analysis also demonstrated a ~ 75% reduction in GFP fluorescence in the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) supporting the idea that the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant is defective in assimilating cholesterol during infection in macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reporter assay data, indicated by 'supporting the idea'.

claim: The majority of genes induced during infection in macrophages and during growth in axenic media containing palmitate were strongly down-regulated in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: The majority of these genes were strongly down-regulated in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant indicating a defect in fatty acid assimilation by the mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from transcriptional profiling, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant has a defect in fatty acid assimilation.
source: The majority of these genes were strongly down-regulated in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant indicating a defect in fatty acid assimilation by the mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on transcriptional profiling data, indicated by 'indicating'.

claim: There was a 10-fold reduction in the amount of Bodipy-C16 assimilated by the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant relative to the wild-type and complemented strains.
source: This analysis revealed a 10-fold reduction in the amount of Bodipy-C16 assimilated by the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant relative to the wild-type and complemented strains (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from flow cytometry, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The decrease in Bodipy-C16 assimilation by the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is not due to a loss of bacterial viability.
source: The decrease in Bodipy-C16 assimilation by the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is not due to a loss of bacterial viability since there was minimal difference in bacterial colony-forming units (CFU) at day 3 of these experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from CFU quantification, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only ~5% of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant cells had identifiable lipid inclusions, while 25% of the wild type and 35% of complemented bacteria had visible cytosolic lipid inclusions during infection in macrophages.
source: Lipid inclusions in Mtb can also be visualized by transmission electron microscopy and we observed that only ~5% of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant cells had identifiable lipid inclusions, while 25% of the wild type and 35% of complemented bacteria had visible cytosolic lipid inclusions during infection in macrophages (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from transmission electron microscopy, with reference to Figure 3C,D.

claim: THL treatment had no effect on the presence of intracellular lipid inclusions in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: Visualizing cytosolic bacterial lipid inclusions with Bodipy-493/503 following THL treatment revealed that THL had no effect on the presence of intracellular lipid inclusions in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from microscopy, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant is unable to utilize both fatty acids and cholesterol during infection in macrophages.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the Mtb ΔlucA::hyg mutant is unable to utilize both fatty acids and cholesterol during infection in macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant has a ~80% and ~95% reduction in its ability to metabolize [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate, respectively.
source: This assay detected a ~80% and ~95% reduction in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant's ability to metabolize the [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate, respectively (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from radiorespirometry assay, with reference to Figure 3E,G.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant has a ~90% and ~95% reduction in its ability to assimilate [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate, respectively.
source: Relative to the wild-type and complemented strains, we observed a ~90% and ~95% reduction in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant's ability to assimilate [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate, respectively (Figure 3F,H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from fatty acid uptake assay, with reference to Figure 3F,H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Inactivating lucA perturbs fatty acid uptake by Mtb, which decreases the bacterium's ability to metabolize fatty acids.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that inactivating lucA perturbs fatty acid uptake by Mtb, which decreases the bacterium's ability to metabolize fatty acids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fatty acid uptake and metabolism data.

claim: Genes in the mce1 locus are strongly induced in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant during infection in macrophages.
source: Analyses of the up-regulated genes in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant during infection in macrophages revealed that genes in the mce1 locus are strongly induced (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from transcriptional profiling, with reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Mce1 functions as a fatty acid transporter in Mtb.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that Mce1 functions as a fatty acid transporter in Mtb.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is subsequently tested and supported by experimental data.

claim: The ΔyrbE1A::hyg mutant displayed a ~70% and~85% reduction in its ability to metabolize [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate, respectively.
source: We found that the ΔyrbE1A::hyg mutant displayed a ~70% and~85% reduction in its ability to metabolize [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate, respectively (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from radiorespirometry assay, with reference to Figure 3E,G.

claim: The ΔyrbE1A::hyg mutant has a ~80% and ~75% reduction in its ability to import [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate.
source: Relative to the wild-type and complemented strains, we detected a ~80% and ~75% reduction in the ΔyrbE1A::hyg mutant's ability to import [14C(U)]-palmitate and [1-14C]-oleate (Figure 3F,H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from fatty acid uptake assay, with reference to Figure 3F,H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: ΔyrbE1A::hyg was still able to metabolize and import cholesterol to wild-type levels.
source: Notably, ΔyrbE1A::hyg was still able to metabolize and import cholesterol to wild-type levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from cholesterol uptake and metabolism assays, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The Δmce1::hyg mutant was defective in fatty acid uptake and metabolism, while this mutant had no detectable defect in cholesterol uptake or metabolism.
source: We found that the Δmce1::hyg mutant was also defective in fatty acid uptake and metabolism, while this mutant had no detectable defect in cholesterol uptake or metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from lipid uptake and metabolism assays, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Mce1 complex functions as a dedicated fatty acid transporter in Mtb.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the Mce1 complex functions as a dedicated fatty acid transporter in Mtb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mce1 mutants.

claim: The mycobacterial 2-hybrid screen identified four sibling clones which all encode an in-frame N-terminal fragment (1–75 aa) of the Rv3492c/Mam4B protein fused to the F1,2 domain of mDHFR.
source: This protein interaction screen identified four sibling clones which all encode an in-frame N-terminal fragment (1–75 aa) of the Rv3492c/Mam4B protein fused to the F1,2 domain of mDHFR.
evidence: This is a direct result from the mycobacterial 2-hybrid screen.

claim: Mam4B is encoded by a gene within the mce4 operon.
source: Mam4B is encoded by a gene within the mce4 operon (Figure 4A,G) and this protein is predicted to function as a subunit of the Mce4 cholesterol transporter complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic organization of the mce4 operon, with reference to Figure 4A,G.

claim: Mam4B is predicted to function as a subunit of the Mce4 cholesterol transporter complex.
source: Mam4B is encoded by a gene within the mce4 operon (Figure 4A,G) and this protein is predicted to function as a subunit of the Mce4 cholesterol transporter complex.
evidence: This is a prediction based on genomic organization and protein domain analysis.

claim: The transmembrane segment of Mam4B is the portion of the Mam4B protein that interacts with LucA.
source: We found that the transmembrane (TM) segment of Mam4B is the portion of the Mam4B protein that interacts with LucA. Co-expressing just the transmembrane domain (1–30 aa) of Mam4B fused to the F1,2 domain of mDHFR (Mam4B(TM)-F1,2) conferred trimethoprim resistance (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the protein interaction assay, with reference to Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LucA physically interacts with Rv0177/Mam1C and Rv0199/OmamA.
source: We found that co-expressing LucA-F3 with full length (FL) versions of Rv0177/Mam1C and Rv0199/OmamA fused to F1,2 conferred trimethoprim resistance (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the protein interaction assay, with reference to Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LucA physically interacts with subunits of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters.
source: These data indicate that LucA physically interacts with subunits of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters and suggests that the LucA protein participates in the function of these complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the protein interaction assay data.

claim: The Δmam4B::hyg mutant is still capable of importing [4-14C]-cholesterol.
source: We found that relative to the wild type and complemented strains the Δmam4B::hyg mutant is still capable of importing [4-14C]-cholesterol (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from cholesterol uptake assay, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The Δmam4B::hyg mutant has an 80% reduction in its ability to metabolize [4-14C]-cholesterol.
source: Importantly, we observed that the Δmam4B::hyg mutant has an obvious cholesterol metabolism defect resulting in an 80% reduction in the mutants ability to metabolize [4-14C]-cholesterol (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from radiorespirometry assay, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The Δmam4B::hyg mutant has no defect in the uptake or metabolism of [1-14C]-oleate.
source: The phenotype of the Δmam4B::hyg strain is specific to cholesterol given that the mutant has no defect in the uptake or metabolism of [1-14C]-oleate (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from oleate uptake and metabolism assays, with reference to Figure 4E,F.

claim: The Rv3492c/Mam4B mutant binds and/or partly imports cholesterol across the Mtb cell envelope.
source: Our interpretation of these observations is that the Rv3492c/Mam4B mutant binds and/or partly imports cholesterol across the Mtb cell envelope and this accounts for the uptake activity that we detect with this strain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, indicated by 'Our interpretation'.

claim: The final translocation of cholesterol across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane is defective in the Δmam4B::hyg mutant.
source: Given that cholesterol is likely not metabolized by Mtb until the substrate reaches the bacterial cytosol we predict that the final translocation of cholesterol across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane is defective in the Δmam4B::hyg mutant and a blockade at this step prevents metabolism of cholesterol in this strain.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental data, indicated by 'we predict'.

claim: Rv3492c/Mam4B is required to complete the process of Mce4-mediated cholesterol internalization by Mtb.
source: Together these data indicate that Rv3492c/Mam4B is required to complete the process of Mce4-mediated cholesterol internalization by Mtb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on the Δmam4B::hyg mutant.

claim: Rv0199/OmamA is involved in cholesterol metabolism in Msm and stabilizes the Mce1 complex in Mtb.
source: Recently, it was demonstrated that Rv0199/OmamA is involved in cholesterol metabolism in Msm and stabilizes the Mce1 complex in Mtb (Perkowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perkowski et al., 2016.

claim: The mce1 genes are expressed in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant to equivalent levels relative to the wild-type and complemented strains.
source: Gene expression analysis by qPCR confirmed that the mce1 genes are expressed in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant to equivalent levels relative to the wild-type and complemented strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from qPCR, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The putative subunits of the Mce1 complex (Mce1A, Mce1D, Mce1E) were completely degraded in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: In contrast, analysis of bacterial lysates revealed that, at the protein level, the putative subunits of the Mce1 complex (Mce1A, Mce1D, Mce1E) were completely degraded in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant (Figure 4G and Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from western blotting, with reference to Figure 4G and Figure 4H.

claim: MceG/Rv0655 functions as a common ATPase to hydrolyze ATP and facilitate nutrient uptake through the Mce transporters in Mtb.
source: It is thought that MceG/Rv0655 functions as a common ATPase to hydrolyze ATP and facilitate nutrient uptake through the Mce transporters in Mtb (Joshi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'It is thought that', supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2006.

claim: MceG is required for optimum growth of Mtb on cholesterol.
source: MceG is required for optimum growth of Mtb on cholesterol and a mutant lacking MceG displays a cholesterol import defect that is equivalent to the cholesterol import defect observed in a mutant lacking Mce4 (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pandey and Sassetti, 2008.

claim: A mutant lacking MceG displays a cholesterol import defect that is equivalent to the cholesterol import defect observed in a mutant lacking Mce4.
source: MceG is required for optimum growth of Mtb on cholesterol and a mutant lacking MceG displays a cholesterol import defect that is equivalent to the cholesterol import defect observed in a mutant lacking Mce4 (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pandey and Sassetti, 2008.

claim: The stability of MceG requires co-expression of the Mce1 and Mce4 permease subunits in mycobacterial cells.
source: Although the role of MceG in fatty acid uptake has not been confirmed, it has been previously established that the stability of MceG requires co-expression of the Mce1 and Mce4 permease subunits in mycobacterial cells (Joshi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2006.

claim: There was a 30% decrease in amount of MceG in the whole-cell lysates of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: Therefore, we quantified MceG levels in the bacterial lysates and observed a 30% decrease in amount of MceG in the whole-cell lysates of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from western blotting, with reference to Figure 4H.

claim: The relative amount of MceG protein decreased by 75% in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant when protein synthesis was suppressed with chloramphenicol.
source: Under this condition, the relative amount of MceG protein decreased by 75% in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from western blotting with chloramphenicol treatment, with reference to Figure 4H.

claim: In the absence of LucA, subunits of the Mce1 transporter complex and the shared MceG ATPase are degraded, possibly due to activity of unknown specific proteases.
source: These results demonstrate that, in the absence of LucA, not only subunits of the Mce1 transporter complex, but also shared MceG ATPase, are degraded, possibly due to activity of unknown specific proteases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the western blotting data, with speculation about the mechanism indicated by 'possibly'.

claim: LucA serves to coordinate the uptake of fatty acids and cholesterol by protecting the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters from degradation.
source: These data provide an explanation for the linked defect in both fatty acid and cholesterol uptake observed in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant and that LucA serves to coordinate the uptake of these nutrients by protecting the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters from degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Deletion of one or both of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters leads to decreased survival of the pathogen in mouse model infection.
source: It is known that deletion of one or both of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters leads to decreased survival of the pathogen in mouse model infection (Joshi et al., 2006), and we predict that both these transporters would be nonfunctional in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2006.

claim: Both the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters would be nonfunctional in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
source: It is known that deletion of one or both of the Mce1 and Mce4 transporters leads to decreased survival of the pathogen in mouse model infection (Joshi et al., 2006), and we predict that both these transporters would be nonfunctional in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental data, indicated by 'we predict'.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant displayed a growth lag that culminates in a 10-fold difference in bacterial counts compared to wild-type and complemented strains over a 7-day infection period in human macrophages.
source: In human macrophages, the ΔlucA::hyg mutant displayed a growth lag that culminates in a 10-fold difference in bacterial counts compared to wild-type and complemented strains over a 7-day infection period (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from macrophage infection assay, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant replicated poorly over a 10-day infection period in resting murine macrophages.
source: A similar phenotype was observed in the resting murine macrophages where the ΔlucA::hyg mutant replicated poorly over a 10-day infection period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from macrophage infection assay, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: In both human and murine macrophages, the final CFU counts for the ΔlucA::hyg mutant remained close to initial inoculum levels.
source: In both human and murine macrophages, the final CFU counts for the ΔlucA::hyg mutant remained close to initial inoculum levels.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from macrophage infection assays.

claim: Mtb requires LucA to sustain maximal growth on cholesterol and/or fatty acid substrates in macrophages.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that Mtb requires LucA to sustain maximal growth on cholesterol and/or fatty acid substrates in macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the macrophage infection data, indicated by 'consistent with the hypothesis'.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant demonstrated a fitness defect in the lung tissues of C57BL/6J mice and did not attain levels of bacterial burden comparable to either the wild type or complemented strains.
source: In the lung tissues of C57BL/6J mice, the ΔlucA::hyg mutant also demonstrated a fitness defect and did not attain levels of bacterial burden comparable to either the wild type or complemented strains.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from mouse infection model.

claim: At day 14 post-infection, 10-fold fewer CFU's of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant were recovered relative to wild-type and the complemented strains in mouse lungs.
source: At day 14 post-infection, 10-fold fewer CFU's of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant were recovered relative to wild-type and the complemented strains.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from mouse infection model.

claim: During the 56-day infection period, growth of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant remained restricted, leading to three- to fivefold reduction in viable ΔlucA::hyg bacteria in mouse lungs.
source: During the remainder of the 56-day infection period, growth of the ΔlucA::hyg mutant remained restricted, leading to three- to fivefold reduction in viable ΔlucA::hyg bacteria (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from mouse infection model, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant induced less pulmonary pathology throughout the entire course of infection in mice.
source: The ΔlucA::hyg mutant also induced less pulmonary pathology throughout the entire course of infection (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from histopathology analysis, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Complementation almost completely restored pathogenicity and lung tissue pathology confirming the specificity of the mutant phenotype to the lucA gene.
source: Complementation almost completely restored pathogenicity and lung tissue pathology confirming the specificity of the mutant phenotype to the lucA gene.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from mouse infection model with complemented strain.

claim: The mechanisms underlying fatty acid uptake by Mtb have remained unknown.
source: Although Mtb's remarkable capacity to assimilate and metabolize lipids is considered a defining characteristic of this pathogen (Cole et al., 1998), the mechanisms underlying fatty acid uptake by Mtb have remained unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, with citation to Cole et al., 1998.

claim: The mycolic acid-containing cell envelope of Mtb constitutes a unique barrier for the import of hydrophobic molecules.
source: The mycolic acid-containing cell envelope of Mtb constitutes a unique barrier for the import of hydrophobic molecules and likely explains why the Mtb genome does not encode canonical fatty acid transporters that are typically found in other bacterial systems (Black et al., 1987; Theodoulou et al., 2016; van den Berg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about the structural properties of the Mtb cell envelope, supported by citations.

claim: The similarities shared across the mce1-4 loci suggest that all these loci encode transporters responsible for the assimilation of hydrophobic substrates in Mtb.
source: Although the functions of proteins encoded in the mce1-mce3 loci are unknown, the similarities shared across the mce1-4 loci suggest that all these loci encode transporters responsible for the assimilation of hydrophobic substrates in Mtb.
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic similarities, indicated by 'suggest'.

claim: Mtb shunts cholesterol-derived methylmalonyl-CoA toward the increased synthesis of methyl-branched, cell wall polyketide lipids during growth in the presence of cholesterol.
source: During growth in the presence of cholesterol Mtb shunts cholesterol-derived methylmalonyl-CoA (originating from propionyl-CoA) toward the increased synthesis of methyl-branched, cell wall polyketide lipids (Griffin et al., 2012; Jain et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Griffin et al., 2012; Jain et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2009).

claim: This metabolic shunting requires that sufficient fatty-acid-derived acyl-AMP primers are available to support biosynthesis of polyketide lipids.
source: This metabolic shunting requires that sufficient fatty-acid-derived acyl-AMP primers are available to support biosynthesis of polyketide lipids (Quadri, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Quadri, 2014.

claim: When excess fatty acids are supplied to infected macrophages, Mtb can enhance the flux of propionyl-CoA into polyketide lipids such as PDIM during infection.
source: When excess fatty acids are supplied to infected macrophages, Mtb can enhance the flux of propionyl-CoA into polyketide lipids such as PDIM during infection (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Coordination of cholesterol and fatty acid uptake by LucA could ensure that balanced levels of these nutrients are maintained for optimized metabolism.
source: Thus, coordination of cholesterol and fatty acid uptake by LucA could ensure that balanced levels of these nutrients are maintained for optimized metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of LucA, indicated by 'could ensure'.

claim: The central carbon and lipid metabolic pathways of Mtb have emerged as potential drug targets.
source: The central carbon and lipid metabolic pathways of Mtb have emerged as potential drug targets (Rhee et al., 2011; VanderVen et al., 2015); therefore, understanding the bottlenecks or weaknesses in these pathways will assist TB drug discovery.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Rhee et al., 2011; VanderVen et al., 2015).

claim: The flux of fatty acids into TAG and central metabolism contributes to drug tolerance in Mtb.
source: Additionally, the flux of fatty acids into TAG and central metabolism contributes to drug tolerance in Mtb (Baek et al., 2011), a phenotype that is further enhanced by immune pressure during in vivo infection (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Baek et al., 2011.

claim: Drug tolerance in Mtb is further enhanced by immune pressure during in vivo infection.
source: Additionally, the flux of fatty acids into TAG and central metabolism contributes to drug tolerance in Mtb (Baek et al., 2011), a phenotype that is further enhanced by immune pressure during in vivo infection (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Targeting the specialized lipid metabolic pathways in Mtb that are involved in fatty acid and cholesterol utilization could be a viable strategy for the development of new drugs that reduce Mtb drug tolerance and augment current TB drug regimens.
source: Targeting the specialized lipid metabolic pathways in Mtb that are involved in fatty acid and cholesterol utilization could be a viable strategy for the development of new drugs that reduce Mtb drug tolerance and augment current TB drug regimens.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about drug development strategy, indicated by 'could be'.

claim: Mtb can co-metabolize simple carbon substrates in vitro.
source: Mtb can co-metabolize simple carbon substrates in vitro (de Carvalho et al., 2010), which suggests that the bacterium has the capacity to utilize fatty acids and cholesterol simultaneously in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: Mtb likely encounters both fatty acids and cholesterol during infection.
source: Mtb likely encounters both fatty acids and cholesterol during infection.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'likely'.

claim: Binding/shuttling of lipids across the Mtb cell envelope may be analogous to what has been proposed for lipid trafficking by Mce proteins across the periplasm of gram-negative bacteria.
source: Binding/shuttling of lipids across the Mtb cell envelope may be analogous to what has been proposed for lipid trafficking by Mce proteins across the periplasm of gram-negative bacteria (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Nakayama and Zhang-Akiyama, 2017; Thong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative comparison indicated by 'may be analogous', supported by citations.

claim: Compensatory systems function to import fatty acids and cholesterol in the absence of Mce1 and Mce4.
source: Lastly, we can detect a residual level of fatty acid and cholesterol uptake and metabolism in mutants lacking Mce1 and Mce4, respectively. It is very likely that compensatory systems function to import these lipids in the absence of Mce1 and Mce4 and we are currently testing this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'It is very likely', based on residual uptake data.

claim: Homology searches based on three-dimensional structures identified a putative protease inhibitor domain within the N-terminus of LucA.
source: Homology searches based on three-dimensional structures identified a putative protease inhibitor domain within the N-terminus of LucA (Kelley et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kelley et al., 2015.

claim: LucA may locally inactivate a protease to maintain the integrity of the transporter complexes.
source: We hypothesize that LucA may locally inactivate a protease to maintain the integrity of the transporter complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis indicated by 'We hypothesize' and 'may'.

claim: Regulating activity of the transport complexes through proteolysis could be a mechanism to rapidly halt nutrient uptake through the Mce transporters.
source: Regulating activity of the transport complexes through proteolysis could be a mechanism to rapidly halt nutrient uptake through the Mce transporters, however such a suggestion will require more research.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'could be' and 'will require more research'.

claim: The Mlep genome contains a single mce locus which is most similar to the mce1 operon found in Mtb.
source: The Mlep genome contains a single mce locus which is most similar to the mce1 operon found in Mtb and Mlep is fully capable of importing and metabolizing palmitate when the bacteria are recovered from animal tissues (Franzblau, 1988).
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic organization of Mlep.

claim: Mlep is fully capable of importing and metabolizing palmitate when the bacteria are recovered from animal tissues.
source: The Mlep genome contains a single mce locus which is most similar to the mce1 operon found in Mtb and Mlep is fully capable of importing and metabolizing palmitate when the bacteria are recovered from animal tissues (Franzblau, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franzblau, 1988.

claim: The Mlep genome also encodes homolog of lucA (ml2337).
source: The Mlep genome also encodes homolog of lucA (ml2337) suggesting that LucA could be central for Mce1 function in this bacterium.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic content of Mlep.

claim: LucA could be central for Mce1 function in Mlep.
source: The Mlep genome also encodes homolog of lucA (ml2337) suggesting that LucA could be central for Mce1 function in this bacterium.
evidence: This is a speculative inference indicated by 'suggesting' and 'could be'.

claim: The Mlep genome does not conserve genes that encode proteins for cholesterol import/metabolism and this bacterium does not metabolize cholesterol.
source: Given that the Mlep genome does not conserve genes that encode proteins for cholesterol import/metabolism and this bacterium does not metabolize cholesterol (Marques et al., 2015), it is likely that ml2337 has one role in Mlep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marques et al., 2015.

claim: ml2337 likely has one role in Mlep.
source: Given that the Mlep genome does not conserve genes that encode proteins for cholesterol import/metabolism and this bacterium does not metabolize cholesterol (Marques et al., 2015), it is likely that ml2337 has one role in Mlep.
evidence: This is a speculative inference indicated by 'it is likely'.

claim: The finding that LucA facilitates fatty acid uptake and stabilizes components of the Mce1 transporter provides additional evidence that Mce1 functions as a fatty acid transporter.
source: The finding that LucA facilitates fatty acid uptake and stabilizes components of the Mce1 transporter provides additional evidence that Mce1 functions as a fatty acid transporter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The fatty acid uptake defect in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is most likely a consequence of the degradation of Mce1 components.
source: Therefore, the fatty acid uptake defect in the ΔlucA::hyg mutant is most likely a consequence of the degradation of Mce1 components (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the protein stability data, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The mce1-4 loci make up four separate operons in the Mtb genome and each operon encodes the putative protein subunits that likely comprise the individual Mce transporters.
source: The mce1-4 loci make up four separate operons in the Mtb genome and each operon encodes the putative protein subunits that likely comprise the individual Mce transporters.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic organization of Mtb, with speculation indicated by 'likely'.

claim: Each Mce transporter is substrate-specific and the individual subunits are predicted to perform discrete roles.
source: It is thought that each Mce transporter is substrate-specific and the individual subunits are predicted to perform discrete roles.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'It is thought' and 'predicted'.

claim: The mce4 operon encodes two putative permease subunits (YrbE4A and YrbE4B), six cell-wall-associated Mce proteins (Mce4A-Mce4F), and two accessory subunits (Mam4A and Mam4B).
source: Specifically, the mce4 operon encodes two putative permease subunits (YrbE4A and YrbE4B), six cell-wall-associated Mce proteins (Mce4A-Mce4F), and two accessory subunits (Mam4A and Mam4B).
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic organization of the mce4 operon.

claim: Mce4 imports cholesterol via a two-step process that involves cholesterol binding/shuttling across the cell wall followed by the final translocation through the cytoplasmic membrane delivering cholesterol into the cytosol.
source: Based on this observation, we propose that Mce4 imports cholesterol via a two-step process that involves cholesterol binding/shuttling across the cell wall followed by the final translocation through the cytoplasmic membrane delivering cholesterol into the cytosol.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental observations, indicated by 'we propose'.

claim: The accessory and permease subunits may participate in the final translocation of cholesterol across the cytoplasmic membrane while the Mce proteins likely participate in the binding/shuttling of cholesterol across the Mtb cell envelope.
source: The accessory and permease subunits may participate in the final translocation of cholesterol across the cytoplasmic membrane while the Mce proteins likely participate in the binding/shuttling of cholesterol across the Mtb cell envelope.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the roles of different subunits, indicated by 'may' and 'likely'.

claim: This two-step mechanism of nutrient uptake may be a generalizable mechanism for all Mce transporters.
source: This two-step mechanism of nutrient uptake may be a generalizable mechanism for all Mce transporters.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization indicated by 'may be'.

claim: LucA is predicted to be recruited to the Mce1 and Mce4 complexes to stabilize or assemble the transporters via interactions with the accessory subunits.
source: Based on this, we predict that LucA is recruited to the Mce1 and Mce4 complexes to stabilize or assemble the transporters via interactions with the accessory subunits.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the protein interaction data, indicated by 'we predict'.

claim: The destabilization of MceG in the ΔlucA::hyg may explain the various nutrient uptake defects in this mutant.
source: Given that MceG is required for cholesterol uptake and is thought to facilitate the import of additional nutrients in Mtb (García-Fernández et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2006; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008), our finding that the MceG protein is also destabilized in the ΔlucA::hyg may explain the various nutrient uptake defects in this mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MceG stability data, indicated by 'may explain', with supporting citations.

claim: Synthesis of Mce proteins can exceed the rates of degradation.
source: It has recently been reported that synthesis of Mce proteins can exceed the rates of degradation (Perkowski et al., 2016) and given that there is negligible difference in the expression of MceG at the RNA level across the strains we used chloramphenicol to suppress protein synthesis in the bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perkowski et al., 2016.
